flagged.evidence: The Definition ends: "It need not exist for an arbitrary action; when it does, it is unique by inclusion." This is false. Take the trivial subgroup H={e} acting on any tree with at least two vertices. Every singleton vertex subtree {v} is a nonempty H-invariant subtree, hence minimal, so there are at least two distinct minimal H-invariant subtrees.

As stated, the lemma is false without a stronger normal-form/transversal hypothesis. In G=<a,t | t a^2 t^{-1}=a^3>, let C_-=<a^2>, u=t, and v=a^{-1}ta. Both u and v are cyclically Britton-reduced of positive stable-letter length 1, and v=a^{-1}ua, so the stated hypotheses hold. But u has only one cyclic permutation. If c=a^{2k} lies in C_-, then c^{-1}tc=a^{-2k}ta^{2k}=a^k t by the defining relation. With transversal S_-={e,a}, the words a^k t and a^{-1} t a are distinct HNN normal forms, so no c in C_- conjugates u to v. The current statement therefore omits a necessary hypothesis.

The theorem repeats the same overbroad positive-length criterion. In G=<a,t | t a^2 t^{-1}=a^3>, the words u=t and v=a^{-1}ta are cyclically Britton-reduced of positive stable-letter length and are conjugate, but no element of C_-=<a^2> conjugates the only cyclic permutation of u to v: for c=a^{2k}, one has c^{-1}tc=a^k t, while a^{-1} t a is a different HNN normal form (for example with S_-={e,a}). So the stated iff fails unless the words are put in a stronger normal-form/transversal setting.
